newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - EW Blanch and Swire Fraser.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - EW Blanch and Swire Fraser.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

Friday's acquisition of Lloyd's broker Swire Fraser by U.S.-based E.W. Blanch for 8.0 million stg reflects two current trends -- consolidation among brokers, and the continued withdrawal of industrial conglomerates from ownership of insurance operations. Swire Pacific last month said it was offloading its stake in insurance underwriters Taikoo Royal Insurance to the Royal & Sun Alliance Group and selling Swire Insurance Holdings to Zurich Insurance. Hardly surprising that it decided to do the same with loss-making Swire Fraser. Swire Pacific said it did not have the capital to invest in insurance and that it wanted to focus on its core areas of property, aviation and industry. This is largely the reason conglomerates pull out of insurance ownership. Only a few days earlier fellow Hong Kong firm Jardine Matheson said it was pulling out of its life insurance business in Asia by selling its 50 percent stake in Jardine CMG Life to Australia-based partner Colonial for US$163 million.
Not so surprising is the acquisition by EW Blanch which, despite having to assume Swire Frasers' 6.2 million stg debt, could work out very well.

For a start Blanch already owned half of Swire Blanch, a joint venture reinsurance broker with offices in Hong Kong, Beijing, Ho Chi Minh City, Singapore and London. Now it will be able to merge Swire Fraser with Swire Blanch, boosting potential earnings without serious change to branding and goodwill.
More importantly it will give Blanch more direct access to the Lloyd's and London markets.

It is also worth noting that Blanch has acquired a group which showed every sign of innovation and divergence despite its tough circumstances. It posted losses after making reserves for real estate (which Swire Fraser no longer occupies) as well as charges associated with the Lloyd's Reconstruction and Renewal plan.

Swire has earned itself a reputation for generating new business ideas. Some failed - such as the idea to offer UK schools "disaster recovery" insurance in the wake of the massacre at a school in Dunblane, Scotland.
However, others such as top-up travel insurance for people hiring cars in the U.S., takeover defence insurance for U.S.

companies and expansion into the big public event insurance market, bolstered by the acquisition of a small operation called 'Sportsafe', have found a ready market. It even insured last year's heavyweight boxing clash between Mike Tyson and Frank Bruno against televisual breakdown.
Another bold move was the formation a year ago of an

international insurance and reinsurance broking division aimed at making Swire Fraser a major force in Asia and South America. This is headed by Godwin Vella and Alan Bennett who were recruited from rival Fenchurch. Swire also recruited brokers in the retail transport and commercial motor fleet sectors. The change of ownership may have been born more out of necessity than desire, but Blanch could well find it makes many gains as a result.
